overview: The team met for the functional design of a new TV remote control. The Marketing Expert set out how features will be gathered and weeded by cost and usability, the 25 Euro impulse-purchase price, and the September launch needed for Christmas sales; research showed users complain that remotes are hard to learn and easily lost. The Project Manager passed on management instructions: the remote controls only the TV, teletext is dropped, and the corporate colour and design must be used. The Industrial Designer explained how a remote works and proposed glowing buttons, a beep and child lock, fun shapes and a clock; the User Interface Designer proposed a power button, timer, child lock, compact shape, safe materials and an alarm clock. The team agreed the target group is everybody with a TV, with extra features for subgroups such as elderly, nervous or young users only if the budget allows. Button design and the cost of variants are still to be worked out; the meeting broke for lunch.

topics.title: Marketing: method, price and timing
points: The Marketing Expert will collect any suggestions first, then eliminate them by design and budget feasibility and prioritise what is most attractive to customers.
The Industrial Designer is consulted on cost and development time, the User Interface Designer on friendliness, look and colour.
The remote should be an attractive impulse purchase at 25 Euros, sold as a Christmas present, so it must reach the market by September.
The sales appeal ("sizzle") matters more than what works best from an engineering view.

topics.title: Research findings and management instructions
points: The Marketing Expert's research found whole-house control is not possible within budget; TV, VCR, stereo and perhaps one more appliance seemed feasible.
The Project Manager relayed management instructions: control only the TV, drop teletext as outdated, keep the corporate image, colour and design.
User complaints: 34 percent say remotes take too long to learn, and remotes are often lost in the room.
The Marketing Expert wants a simple, intuitive remote with few buttons, a light-emitting locator and perhaps a beep.
Suggested marketing motto: "we put fashion in electronics".

topics.title: Industrial design: how a remote works and extra features
points: A chip (integrated circuit) takes power from a battery, reads button presses and sends infrared signals to the device; multiple devices would each need to recognise the frequency, which is hard.
Proposed features: fluorescent buttons that glow in the dark, a beep when many buttons are pressed at once, a child lock.
Fun shapes and colours, for example animal shapes; the Industrial Designer and Project Manager said a different mould would not add much cost.

The Marketing Expert asked about the same electronics in several shapes, such as a sexy one for adults and an animal for children; the Project Manager said it needs a budget check but is fun in principle.

Multi-mode buttons would reduce the button count but add complexity; the Marketing Expert and Project Manager worried about learning and elderly users with arthritic hands, and suggested differently shaped buttons for touch, and clear text.
A clock display, which the Industrial Designer said costs nothing extra; the Marketing Expert and Project Manager liked it.
Components: buttons over switches, a light that turns on when the TV is on to help find the remote, infrared bulbs, battery, chip, wires and a case or holder.
The Industrial Designer used the company website for ideas.

topics.title: User interface: requested features
points: Main purpose is controlling the TV from a distance: power button, infrared or radio signal, channel and volume changes.
A timer to switch the TV on for a programme or off at a set time, for example a parental switch-off at ten o'clock.
Child lock on particular channels.
Compact, with many buttons; personal preference for a T shape.
Materials safe for skin and allergies, no sharp edges for children.
An alarm clock, which the Industrial Designer and Marketing Expert thought fine; fluorescent buttons that glow differently.
Remotes use infrared or radio waves.

topics.title: Target group and functions
points: The Project Manager said the meeting must decide the target group and the working design.
Target group is everybody with a TV, with subgroups: elderly people with limited finger movement, nervous people, and possibly children.
The Marketing Expert noted children drive purchases; the Project Manager said children can be addressed through shape and colour.
The User Interface Designer proposed a core design for ages ten to forty with add-on buttons for others, and noted a family buys one remote, not three.
The Industrial Designer proposed separate remotes, such as a larger one with big buttons for the elderly; electronics cost would not change.
The Project Manager suggested removable cases like mobile phone covers, with a spare in the box and extra colour packs sold separately; others liked it.

Conclusion: one remote for everyone with a TV, with subgroup features only if money permits; the Industrial Designer suggested roughly seventy percent standard and thirty percent variants. Points may be revisited next meeting.
